title_en: Guiding Case No. 235: Application of S Shipping Co., Ltd. for Recognition of a Foreign Court Civil Judgment
ruling_gist_en: When a people's court examines an application or request for recognition and enforcement of a civil judgment or ruling of a foreign court and determines whether a reciprocal relationship exists, it shall not take the prior recognition and enforcement by the relevant foreign court of a civil judgment or ruling of a people's court as a necessary condition. If, according to the law of the relevant country, a civil judgment or ruling made by a people's court can be recognized and enforced by the courts of that country, and that country has no precedent of refusing to recognize and enforce a people's court's judgment or ruling on the ground of absence of a reciprocal relationship, it may be determined that a reciprocal relationship exists between China and that country for the recognition and enforcement of civil judgments and rulings.

full_text_en:
Guiding Case No. 235: S Shipping Co., Ltd. v. Mouhua Logistics Holding (Group) Co., Ltd. — Application for Recognition of Foreign Court Civil Judgment

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on November 25, 2024)

Keywords
Civil; application for recognition of foreign court civil judgment; reciprocal relationship; case-by-case review; factual reciprocity; legal reciprocity

Ruling Gist

When a people's court reviews an application or request for recognition and enforcement of a foreign court's civil judgment or ruling and determines whether a reciprocal relationship exists, it shall not take prior recognition and enforcement by the relevant foreign court of a civil judgment or ruling of a people's court as a necessary condition. If, under the laws of the relevant country, a civil judgment or ruling rendered by a people's court can be recognized and enforced by the courts of that country, and that country has no precedent of refusing to recognize and enforce a judgment or ruling of a people's court on the ground that no reciprocal relationship exists, it may be determined that a reciprocal relationship exists between China and that country for the recognition and enforcement of civil judgments and rulings.

Basic Facts

On March 5, 2010, S Shipping Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "S Shipping") entered into three time charter parties with Mouhua (Hong Kong) Shipping Company, leasing three vessels to Mouhua (Hong Kong) Shipping Company. On March 25, 2010, Mouhua Logistics Holding (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Mouhua Logistics") issued three letters of guarantee to S Shipping, providing guarantees for Mouhua (Hong Kong) Shipping Company's performance under the aforesaid charter parties. All three letters of guarantee stipulated that English law would apply and that disputes would be submitted to the High Court of England and Wales in London for trial. Because Mouhua (Hong Kong) Shipping Company delayed in paying charter hire, S Shipping filed an action against Mouhua Logistics in the High Court of England and Wales pursuant to the letters of guarantee. Mouhua Logistics appeared and defended the action. On March 18, 2015, the High Court of England and Wales rendered judgment [2015] EWHC 718 (Comm) in favor of S Shipping. Subsequently, the High Court of England and Wales also determined the amount of the debt and costs, issuing orders on April 27, 2015, and October 3, 2016, a final costs certificate on November 1, 2016, and an amended order on May 17, 2018. Mouhua Logistics appealed to the Court of Appeal of England and Wales. On October 7, 2016, the Court of Appeal of England and Wales rendered judgment [2016] EWCA Civ 982, dismissing Mouhua Logistics' appeal. The Court of Appeal subsequently issued orders on October 7, 2016, and May 8, 2017. Mouhua Logistics failed to perform the obligations determined by the effective judgments. S Shipping then requested a Chinese court to recognize the aforesaid judgments of the High Court of England and Wales and the Court of Appeal of England and Wales, as well as a series of related court orders. Mouhua Logistics argued that China and the United Kingdom have neither concluded nor acceded to any international treaty on mutual recognition and enforcement of court judgments and rulings, nor have they established a corresponding reciprocal relationship.

Judgment

The Shanghai Maritime Court rendered a civil ruling (2018) Hu 72 Xie Wai Ren No. 1 on March 17, 2022: recognizing the judgment of the High Court of England and Wales rendered on March 18, 2015, in case [2015] EWHC 718 (Comm), and the orders made therein on April 27, 2015, and October 3, 2016, the final costs certificate made on November 1, 2016, and the amended order made on May 17, 2018; recognizing the judgment of the Court of Appeal of England and Wales rendered on October 7, 2016, in case [2016] EWCA Civ 982, and the orders made therein on October 7, 2016, and May 8, 2017.

Reasoning

This case concerns an application for recognition of a foreign court civil judgment. Pursuant to Article 289 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (as amended in 2021), when a people's court reviews an application or request for recognition and enforcement of a legally effective judgment or ruling rendered by a foreign court, it shall conduct the review in accordance with international treaties concluded or acceded to by the People's Republic of China, or in accordance with the principle of reciprocity. Since China and the United Kingdom have neither concluded nor acceded to any international treaty on mutual recognition and enforcement of court civil judgments and rulings, the principle of reciprocity shall serve as the basis for reviewing whether to recognize the UK court judgments.

The principle of reciprocity is a concrete manifestation of the principle of equality and mutual benefit in private international law. The Civil Procedure Law of China does not limit the principle of reciprocity to requiring that the relevant foreign court first recognize and enforce a civil judgment or ruling of a Chinese court. Of course, if the relevant foreign court has precedents of recognizing and enforcing civil judgments or rulings of Chinese courts, a factual reciprocal relationship for recognition and enforcement of civil judgments and rulings may naturally be found to exist between China and that country. However, even in the absence of such precedents, if, under the laws of the country of the foreign court that rendered the judgment, the conditions for recognizing and enforcing judgments or rulings of other countries' courts are substantially the same as or more lenient than those provided by Chinese law, it may be determined that, under equivalent circumstances, a civil judgment or ruling rendered by a Chinese court can be recognized and enforced by the courts of that country. Against this backdrop, if there is no precedent where the courts of that country have refused to recognize and enforce a civil judgment or ruling of a Chinese court on the ground that no reciprocal relationship exists, it may be determined that a legal reciprocal relationship exists between China and that country.

In this case, the applicant, S Shipping, did not provide evidence of precedents where UK courts have recognized and enforced civil judgments or rulings of Chinese courts, and thus could not prove the existence of a factual reciprocal relationship between China and the UK for recognition and enforcement of civil judgments and rulings. However, from the specific practice of UK courts, when a judgment or ruling of a foreign court seeks recognition and enforcement in the UK, it must, in accordance with UK common law rules, be based on the foreign court's judgment or ruling and a fresh action must be brought in a UK court. If the conditions for recognition and enforcement are satisfied, the UK court will render a judgment substantially identical to the original judgment, which will then be enforced under the procedures prescribed by UK law. This is also a common practice in common law countries. According to UK law, the existence of a relevant treaty is not a necessary condition for recognizing and enforcing foreign court judgments and rulings. There is no evidence that there are legal obstacles to the recognition and enforcement of Chinese court judgments and rulings in UK courts, nor has it been found that UK courts have ever refused to recognize and enforce Chinese court judgments and rulings on the ground that no reciprocal relationship exists. Therefore, it may be determined that a legal reciprocal relationship exists between China and the UK. The UK court judgments involved in this case do not violate the basic principles of Chinese law or harm the national sovereignty, security, or public interest of China.

In summary, although China and the United Kingdom have neither concluded nor acceded to any international treaty on mutual recognition and enforcement of court civil judgments and rulings, the UK court judgments involved in this case may be recognized on the basis of the principle of reciprocity.

Following the rendering of this ruling recognizing the UK court judgments, the High Court of England and Wales recognized two judgments of the Hangzhou Intermediate People's Court of Zhejiang Province in December 2022.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 299 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (Article 289 of the Civil Procedure Law as amended in 2021 is applied in this case).
